meta.title: Who originally recorded "Fly Me to the Moon"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Frank Sinatra. Kaye Ballard recorded it first, for Decca in April 1954, as a B-side titled "In Other Words." Sinatra's version came in 1964.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Fly Me to the Moon'?
meta.ogDescription: Kaye Ballard cut it first for Decca in April 1954, as a B-side called "In Other Words." Sinatra's famous Basie version arrived in 1964.

answer.label: Not a Frank Sinatra original — a 1954 Kaye Ballard single for Decca
answer.originalArtistDates: 1925–2019 · American singer, comedian and Broadway star
answer.sourceLine: Frank Sinatra’s swaggering Count Basie recording is so total a possession of this song that most people assume he made it first. He didn’t. Bart Howard wrote it in 1954 under the title “In Other Words,” and the first commercial recording was Kaye Ballard’s, issued by Decca in April 1954 as the B-side of her single “Lazy Afternoon.” Sinatra’s version came in 1964, on the Reprise album It Might as Well Be Swing.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Decca Records
original.released: Issued by Decca Records (catalogue 29114) in April 1954 as the B-side of Kaye Ballard’s single “Lazy Afternoon,” a song from The Golden Apple, the Broadway show she was starring in. It carried the song’s original title, “In Other Words.”
original.charted: Did not chart. It was a B-side, reviewed but not promoted — Billboard’s 8 May 1954 notice called it a love song sung with feeling by Miss Ballard, and that was largely that.
original.cover: Frank Sinatra recorded it with the Count Basie Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Quincy Jones, for the Reprise album It Might as Well Be Swing (FS 1012), released August 1964. It was an album track rather than a hit single; the album reached No. 13 on the Billboard Top LPs chart. The song’s only sizeable US chart placing had come earlier, with Joe Harnell’s bossa nova instrumental at No. 14 on the Hot 100 in February 1963.

docMeta.dd: April 1954, as the B-side of “Lazy Afternoon”

trail: The Wikipedia article on the song ↗ dates Bart Howard’s composition to 1954 under the title “In Other Words,” names Kaye Ballard’s Decca release of April 1954 as the first commercial recording, and cites a Billboard review of 8 May 1954.
The Songwriters Hall of Fame profile ↗ independently describes Ballard’s Decca record as the first commercial recording and traces the 1963 title change to Peggy Lee.
The physical disc survives: the Internet Archive’s preservation transfer of Decca 29114 ↗ logs the label, catalogue number, April 1954 date and matrix number W86143T3A.
In 2026 the Library of Congress added the recording to the National Recording Registry, listed as “Fly Me to the Moon (In Other Words)” — Kaye Ballard (1954) ↗.

authors.name: Kaye Ballard
authors.heading: Kaye Ballard
authors.metaLine: 1925–2019 · American singer, comedian and Broadway star
authors.bio: Born Catherine Gloria Balotta in Cleveland to Italian immigrant parents, Ballard came up as a musical comedienne — a stint with Spike Jones and His City Slickers, then the New York cabaret circuit. In early 1954 she was starring on Broadway in The Golden Apple, and for the flipside of her “Lazy Afternoon” single she picked a new song by the pianist and MC at the Blue Angel club. She is best remembered today for television — The Mothers-in-Law, Hollywood Squares — but the Library of Congress inducted this 1954 single into the National Recording Registry in 2026.

authors.name: Frank Sinatra
authors.heading: Frank Sinatra
authors.bio: Sinatra cut the song in 1964 with the Count Basie Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Quincy Jones, for the Reprise album It Might as Well Be Swing. He recast a tender cabaret waltz as a hard-swinging 4/4 showpiece, and the arrangement is so definitive that it effectively rewrote the song for everyone who came after. It then travelled with NASA’s Apollo programme and became the record most people mean when they name the title. The only error in the popular account is chronological.

authors.name: Bart Howard
authors.heading: Bart Howard
authors.bio: Born Howard Joseph Gustafson in Burlington, Iowa, Howard accompanied Mabel Mercer in the late 1940s and spent the 1950s as MC and intermission pianist at New York’s Blue Angel. He wrote this song in 1954 as “In Other Words,” and in 1963 agreed to retitle it after the phrase everyone was already using. By 1964 he reckoned it had been recorded more than a hundred times, and its royalties supported him for the rest of his life. The Songwriters Hall of Fame named it a Towering Song in 1999.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong originator
misattribution.intro: Sinatra’s 1964 recording is so dominant that it is routinely treated as the song’s point of origin. The record itself is a decade older, and came out under a different title.

items.why: His Reprise recording with the Count Basie Orchestra, arranged by Quincy Jones, appeared on It Might as Well Be Swing in August 1964. It is the version almost everyone means — but it is not the first.

Ballard made the first commercial recording, issued by Decca (29114) in April 1954 as the B-side of “Lazy Afternoon,” under the song’s original title “In Other Words.” Billboard reviewed it on 8 May 1954.

Howard wrote words and music in 1954 while working as MC and intermission pianist at New York’s Blue Angel, where Ballard was a familiar performer. Neither Ballard nor Sinatra had a hand in writing it.

items.tag: Why it is not called “In Other Words”
items.why: Lee recorded the song in 1960 and performed it on The Ed Sullivan Show, then persuaded Howard to make “Fly Me to the Moon” the official title in 1963 — before Sinatra ever recorded it.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Bart Howard in 1954 as “In Other Words”; first recorded by Kaye Ballard, Decca, April 1954; made famous by Frank Sinatra in 1964.

context.heading: How a B-side became a Sinatra song
lead: The original is not obscure because it was bad. Ballard’s Decca record is a straight, unhurried cabaret ballad in 3/4 — roughly two and a quarter minutes of it — and it did exactly what a B-side was built to do in 1954, which is sit quietly behind the A-side and be forgotten. The A-side, “Lazy Afternoon,” was the commercial proposition; it came from the Broadway show Ballard was starring in.

What eclipsed it was not Sinatra directly but a chain of interpreters. Peggy Lee sang it on her 1960 album Pretty Eyes and on The Ed Sullivan Show, and it was Lee who persuaded Howard to change the title officially in 1963. Joe Harnell’s bossa nova instrumental was the song’s first genuine chart hit, reaching No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1963 and winning a Grammy. Only after all that did Sinatra, Basie and Quincy Jones arrive and put a lid on the matter.
detailsBody: 1954 — Bart Howard writes the song as “In Other Words.”
April 1954 — Kaye Ballard’s recording is issued by Decca (catalogue 29114) as the B-side of “Lazy Afternoon.” Billboard reviews it on 8 May 1954.
1960 — Peggy Lee records it for her album Pretty Eyes and later performs it on The Ed Sullivan Show.
1962–63 — Joe Harnell’s bossa nova instrumental reaches No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 23 February 1963 and wins a Grammy at the 5th Annual Grammy Awards.
1963 — at Peggy Lee’s urging, Howard officially retitles the song “Fly Me to the Moon.”
August 1964 — Frank Sinatra’s version appears on the Reprise album It Might as Well Be Swing, with the Count Basie Orchestra, arranged by Quincy Jones.
2026 — the Library of Congress adds Ballard’s 1954 single to the National Recording Registry.
context.pull: A B-side did its job perfectly: nobody noticed it.

listen.what: Kaye Ballard, “In Other Words” — the April 1954 Decca original, transferred from the 78.
listen.source: Not a fan upload: this is the Internet Archive’s 78rpm / George Blood, L.P. preservation collection, a direct transfer of the physical Decca 29114 disc with matrix number W86143T3A logged in the item metadata. Its running time of 137.6 seconds matches the 134-second length MusicBrainz records for the recording on the 1954 “In Other Words / Lazy Afternoon” single, the small excess being 78 lead-in and run-out — so this is the 1954 record, not a later re-recording.
